paras: The Evansville race riot of 1903 was a series of white mob attacks in Evansville, Indiana, on July 5 and 6, 1903, first on the county jail to lynch Lee Brown (Robert Lee), a Black man accused of killing a policeman, and then on Black residents. On July 6 militia guarding the jail fired into the crowd, killing ten by the coroner's count, while many Black residents fled. Black papers stressed that no white woman figured in the case and saw mob violence spreading north.

According to wire reports, on Friday night, July 3, Brown quarreled with another Black man, fetched a revolver, and shot Patrolman Louis N. Massey when the officer stopped him; Massey wounded Brown dangerously and died the next night.

About 2:30 on Sunday morning, July 5, a mob of about a hundred men and boys battered down a jail gate with a telephone pole. Sheriff C. W. Kratz called the police, who pushed back this and a second attack without firing, and then took Brown to Vincennes. During the day white boys attacked Black men, and armed Black groups gathered near the jail.

By 11 that night nearly 3,000 people stood before the jail; two committees searched it and found Brown gone, but the crowd shouted 'Go get the nigger!' After looting hardware stores for guns, the mob set out in search of Black people and, the Indianapolis Journal reported, fired on any it saw. It shot up Budd Fruit's resort, where Cain McGee was wounded, wrecked a Baptisttown saloon, beat several Black men nearly to death, and at dawn set out for powder to blow up Baptisttown. Black men were in turn reported to have shot a white boy named Logan.

On Monday the grand jury indicted Brown for murder. That evening about a thousand people surrounded the jail, held by a National Guard company and about a hundred deputies, and stoned the soldiers. At 10:30 the crowd pressed forward, a shot was fired, and the defenders fired about 300 shots into it; fifteen-year-old Hazel Allman, watching with her parents, was among the dead.

General W. J. McKee arrived on July 7 with about 400 troops, who stayed until July 15. Baptisttown emptied, Black families camped armed along the Newburg road, and Black workers left the streets at sundown on their ministers' advice. A letter to the Colored American described the destruction of Black property, and many who fled had not returned weeks later.

Five men were arrested on riot indictments and bonded, while nine of ten men fined for carrying concealed weapons were Black. The St. Paul Appeal put the number indicted at 88, 'said' to be more than half Afro-Americans; no verdict appears in the coverage examined. Coroner Walling found that ten people died of rifle wounds inflicted by 'unknown persons' during the attack on the jail.

Governor Winfield T. Durbin stopped Brown's return to Evansville, and Brown died untried in the Jeffersonville reformatory in late July of Massey's bullet. His wife, who fled the night of the riot, was reported killed by a train near Madisonville, Kentucky.

The first wire dispatches, headed 'Race War in Indiana. Whites Kill Negroes,' called Brown 'the negro slayer' and described armed Black companies 'threatening to kill all white people.' The Indianapolis Journal called Brown 'a Negro Murderer' but also reported the mob firing on Black people and the flight of Black families.

Black weeklies reprinted the wire, the Indianapolis Freeman under 'Innocent Girl Killed.' Editorially, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted the New York Post's 'nothing less than anarchy,' and the Sedalia Times wrote of 'white savagery.' The Sedalia Conservator defended Black self-defense, and the Plaindealer printed Paul Laurence Dunbar's protest linking Evansville to Belleville and Wilmington.

Several Black papers welcomed the militia's fire: the St. Paul Appeal quoted a sermon on 'the Evansville cure,' and the Iowa Bystander wished the same 'dose' on Southern mobs. The Freeman deplored Brown's crime but blamed 'the anti-Negro spirit,' and it and the Colored American praised Durbin.
Death counts ran from six to twelve, and first-night wire reports of Black people killed were contradicted by the Indianapolis Journal; no Black dead is named. Soldiers said the rioters fired first.

reader.title: Evansville race riot of 1903
bases: After failing to take Lee Brown from the county jail, white mobs fired on Black people wherever seen, shot up Black resorts and set out to blow up Baptisttown, driving many Black residents from the city (A2, A4, A13).

The Indianapolis Journal's own correspondents, several independent wire versions and Black-press reports agree on the jail attacks, the mob's assaults on Black residents and the militia fire (A1, A2, A4, A10, A28).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal correspondent
accounts.gist: Two Sunday-morning jail attacks repulsed by police; Lee moved to Vincennes; that night the mob, convinced he was gone, hunted Black people, firing on any it saw; Black men also fired on whites.

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: A mob shouting 'Death to all negroes!' broke into the jail; two Black men and a Black woman killed; an armed Black company marched threatening whites.

accounts.label: Soldiers' version
accounts.gist: The crowd pressed on the jail, stoned soldiers, a shot was fired and the defenders fired about 300 shots; soldiers said the rioters fired first, the rioters would not talk.

accounts.label: Coroner's verdict
accounts.gist: Ten dead from rifles 'in the hands of unknown persons' during the riotous attack on the jail and militia on July 6.

accounts.label: Black editorial view
accounts.gist: A Black man's crime became the pretext for an attack on all Black residents in a Northern city, with no charge involving a white woman.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Race War in Indiana. Whites Kill Negroes' and 'Negro Shot Policeman'; Brown called 'the negro slayer' and 'a Negro Murderer'; armed Black bands reported as threatening all whites, while the mob's attacks on Black people were also reported.
Second-day coverage centered on the militia fire and the white dead: 'Militia Kills Seven', 'Martial Law in Evansville', 'Keeping Order at Evansville'.
Editorials called the mob anarchy and 'white savagery', stressed no white woman figured in the case, and defended Black self-defense.
The Freeman deplored Brown's crime while blaming 'the anti-Negro spirit' and praising the Governor; others welcomed the militia's fire as 'the Evansville cure' and 'that much justice'.
Wire accounts ran in the Western World, Iowa Bystander, St. Louis Palladium and Indianapolis Freeman, the last under 'Innocent Girl Killed'.

record_check.record: Lee Brown plus about 30 names, mostly people shot by the militia
record_check.dossier: Brown was the accused and the mob's target; the Black victims of the mob are mostly unnamed (beaten men, Cain McGee, Henry Black); the named dead were in the crowd at the jail, shot by militia and deputies.
Contested: early wire reported two Black men and a Black woman killed; the Indianapolis Journal found no one killed; no Black dead named.
Several, unnumbered: Black men beaten nearly to death, Cain McGee shot, Brown wounded by Massey.
Six to twelve in the crowd by differing counts, ten per coroner (race unstated), plus Patrolman Massey; Brown later died of his wound.
Brown was in the county jail and the mob tried to take him, but he was removed to Vincennes before it got in; he was never taken.
Mobs of white men and boys; five named men arrested on riot indictments.
Bombing was threatened (march for powder to blow up Baptisttown), not carried out; no arson reported in the opened articles; killing of Black people contested.

record_check.dossier: Not found in the opened articles; reports give the mob's motive as rage at failing to lynch Brown, with claims of armed Black bands and Black men shooting whites.

info: Patrolman Massey shot Friday night, July 3; jail attacks early Sunday, July 5; mob attacks on Black residents Sunday night, July 5-6; militia fire on the mob Monday, July 6, about 10:30 p.m.
Vanderburg County jail, downtown streets and the Black district of Baptisttown, Evansville, Indiana

The mob's target was Lee Brown, also called Robert Lee, held for killing a patrolman; after failing to find him the mob attacked Black residents generally, mostly unnamed: several beaten, Cain McGee shot in the arm, Black resorts shot up, homes fired into, families driven out.
Brown was accused of shooting and killing Patrolman Louis N. Massey on July 3 after a quarrel with another Black man; indicted for murder July 6.
Mobs of white men and boys; five men arrested on indictments for the Sunday-night riot (Richard Grosbeck, A. P. Cardwell, J. T. Zeigler, William Trimble, James Steele).

Contested: first wire reports said two Black men and an unknown Black woman were killed; the Indianapolis Journal reported next day that so far as learned no one was killed Sunday night. No Black person killed by the mob is named.

Brown, moved to Vincennes and then the Jeffersonville reformatory, died there in late July of the lung wound from Massey's bullet, before trial. No report of a verdict against any rioter was found in the opened coverage.
